We know that everything on the web is a box by default, but you’ll find many animated s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real , you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble wearing HTML/CSS can. has a strict no .html policy.

In a recent development, the tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

According to recent reports, besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

If you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to initiative an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

According to recent reports, SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated rapidly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:.

That’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can swiftly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a fresh animation, let’s blueprint all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

Industry observers note that I like to proposal my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

According to recent reports, for now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:.

See the Pen [colorAndOpacityChange [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016dc-399c-7652-b172-4cd4663746b9) by Johan Grobler.

The notable thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

A substantial part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

In a recent development, let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

Using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

See the Pen [syncbase.end [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/emgwwGJ) by Johan Grobler.

It has been revealed that something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

See the Pen [syncbase.begin [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/xbgooXq) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

Recent findings suggest that let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:.

Recent findings suggest that browsers have wide support for the prefers-reduced-motion media feature and Val Head explains this in depth in another article. We definitely want to respect this user preference as we consider moving things around. In fact, consider it non-negotiable.

There are various approaches to adhering to a user’s prefers-reduced-motion setting when it comes to SMIL. Each with its pros and cons. Evaluating early on what’s going to work best for your use case could save you a partial rewrite down the line.

For example, we could consider using a element instead of a plain because supports multiple elements that can be used as fallbacks in a media attribute for reduced motion preferences.

Or one SVG file with an inline CSS @media query that uses display: none to swap between versions. That said, it’s an approach that might cause trouble in various environments. But browsers are continuously changing, and this might not be an concern in the future.

You might also consider a CSS background-image instead because we can wrap that style in a media query — @media (prefers-reduced-motion) — that sets a static image as the fallback for reduced motion preferences.

There are even more options we can turn to! For example, SVG’s element can also be used to swap things out for motion preferences.

Or, if we prefer everything bundled together, we can use JavaScript .matchMedia() and the handy SMIL DOM interface to control which animations start instead of completely switching out files.

For this, I’m avoiding any motion and sticking to opacity animations, which tend to cause less trouble. For a non-interactive animation like this, we can load it in an tag. When we add motion, we can go the route to show the most appropriate version of our animation.

We’re going to do our own version of the classic three-dot spinner:.

See the Pen [StaticDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016e5-c44d-75b3-bbb2-3eca2f83932d) by Johan Grobler.

Recent findings suggest that SVG wizards might be able to do everything directly in a text editor. I recommend using a graphic editor like Inkscape if you’re having trouble visualizing how the markup will be rendered. Once again, Andy Clarke has a great article about his process for optimizing and structuring his own drawings.

Sources indicate that note: There’s a gotcha with Inkscape. Setting what you would expect to be an element’s ID via the Layers window actually sets the value of a metadata attribute used internally by Inkscape. Use Inkscape’s object properties or XML editor window to set the true element’s ID. Your mileage may vary with a different editor. Also, in Inkscape, remember to save the file as optimized SVG when the drawing is done to strip away unneeded metadata.

Industry observers note that OK, so we’re sticking with the opacity animation idea. The dots are going to fade in and out. We’ll use separate tags for those. Six tags in total.

Our naming scheme is going to be straightforward: we’ll call them #fadeIn and #fadeOut, and to differentiate between each pair of tags, we’ll postfix the tag’s ID with either Left, Middle or Right. Try to follow a convention that makes sense to you when coming up with your own IDs.

The fade-in tag for the dot on the left:.

And the fade-out for the middle dot:.

We have an infinite number of ways in which we could space these six animations in time. Let’s look at a couple of choice examples alongside their timing charts to see how changing the arrangement of the parts impacts the visual effect of the whole animation.

To narrow our choices a bit, all of the tags will use the same dur value, and none of the syncbase values will have offsets.

According to recent reports, for someone coming from a culture that reads from left to right, the dots appearing on screen along the same pattern would feel natural. Let’s also start with all the dots fading out together at the end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion1 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ec-0b1b-731e-bf44-2dd45b7c075f) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values stagger the fade-ins and restart the loop when the dots have disappeared:.

It has been revealed that since all the fade-outs end at the same time, it is an arbitrary choice which one we use to restart the loop. We’ll consider #fadeOutLeft as the primary animation here and also synchronize the other fade-outs to it with the syncbase value fadeOutLeft.begin. Later, if we want to move the fade-outs in time, all we do is change when #fadeOutLeft starts.

Instead of a group fade-out, we could stagger them just like the fade-ins:.

Without adding an offset, there are a couple of points in time we could start #fadeOutLeft at. If it starts on fadeInRight.end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion2 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-1be0-7359-a8ce-1d45194ed50a) by Johan Grobler.

The visual effect is subtly changed by moving up a spot and starting #fadeOutLeft on fadeInMiddle.end instead:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion3 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-f4d9-745b-a89f-2ff35d898589) by Johan Grobler.

We can see from the charts that we could try moving up a spot further to fadeInLeft.end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion4 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-07f8-732a-966d-c295618c60d7) by Johan Grobler.

How about starting the sequence with a fade-out:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion5 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-b6a5-7078-a73c-217459f53e20) by Johan Grobler.

You might prefer to start with the dot in the middle:.

See the Pen [centerFirstDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f2-5f78-70a2-a948-f030c147fbe3) by Johan Grobler.

As you iterate on your animation, timing charts are a great way to keep track of your work, and they make visual comparison between versions possible. And by drawing a timing chart, you might even see a pattern in the timing between the parts of the animations that you might otherwise have missed.

It has been revealed that as you animate more elements and properties, it gets harder to keep track of what starts when. To see how timing charts can help you make sense of things, let’s build on the basic spinner:.

See the Pen [staticDotsWithClipPaths [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f4-f99c-7779-b526-1265ecf5619b) by Johan Grobler.

It has been revealed that I’ve added a for each dot to the drawing. We’ll move those into to a tag and remove the fill="white". As the animation runs, the rectangles are going to move over the dots for a different approach to animating the stroke than by animating stroke-dashoffset.

We only need a single for all three dots, but it adds structure to the document, and it’s good practice to wrap it, and similar tags, in a tag:.

Remember to set the clip path for the s. Either with CSS or using the clip-path attribute:.

Because the dots now have a stroke added, to leave their size unchanged, we need to compensate by subtracting half the value of stroke-width from r:.

In a recent development, that’s all the changes the graphics need. Have a look at the animated version with its timing chart, then we’ll look in more detail at the changes that have been made to the animation:.

See the Pen [clipPathDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f8-73b0-707a-b21a-7aa07fb194b2) by Johan Grobler.

There’s a new animation, #moveClipPathLeft, that starts the whole sequence, and to tweak the animation’s rhythm a bit, there’s a 1s delay between when the fade-outs end and the loop restarts:.

It has been revealed that you could use s to move the rectangles instead, but we need to move them back to their starting positions at the end for a smooth restart of the animation. You’ll need to take into account which tags can animate and set which data types if you do decide to animate the transform attribute instead of translating the rectangles with the y attribute.

To change things up, the for the middle dot moves down:.

We’re also using the fill-opacity property instead of the opacity property for the fade-ins, and they’ve been synchronized to start once a dot’s clipping has finished moving:.

The fade-outs still use the normal opacity property, so both the fill and stroke fade out together. Because this arrangement is set up to use a group fade-out at the end, there are a few places the markup could be optimized. One of them is dropping the fill="freeze" to automatically reset the dot’s opacity back to its starting value once the tag finishes running:.

For the tags that did use fill="freeze", we’ll use tags to reset those properties back to their starting values. I’ve simplified the chart a little by lumping those tags together. Because these tags don’t have a duration over which they act, on the chart I’ve drawn the start and end markers over each other.

To reset the fill-opacity on the left dot:.

If you use fill="freeze" with the fade-outs, you’ll need an extra for each dot to reset the middle dot’s opacity:.

Recent findings suggest that the last thing we need to do is move the clipping rectangles back to their starting positions. For the right :.

That’s just one of the possible timing variations, and most of what you’ll need to try some of the others, as we did with the basic spinner, is already in place. You might want to have a try at coming up with a couple of your own alternate timings.

It has been revealed that to sum things up, we know that balancing the different stages of an animation can be difficult at best, and untenable at worst. Any time we get into multi-step animations that exceed one or two steps, it’s a form of orchestration. You’re almost building a Rube Goldberg machine of markup. And using a timing chart is a strategy I use that I hope will help you in your projects as well. They are outlines of what to expect and when, allowing you to map things out in a way that not only helps plan your code, but also makes future updates and maintenance a lot more bearable than going into it without a plan.

According to recent reports, while a timing chart can’t reduce the complexity of the markup, it can give a good overview of what should happen when. Timing charts are definitely not limited to SMIL animations. Unfortunately, syncbase values are, and they can still help even if you’re going to use a different approach to implementing your animation.

I highly recommend checking out Andy’s other articles on Smashing Magazine. There’s even more stuff on combining CSS and SVG.

Yosra Emad wrote a great article on creating animations with multiple steps in CSS, and you might want to try drawing a few timing charts as you read through it.

When you’re ready to start adding those in-between lines to your timing chart, Nash Vail’s article on easing dives deep into the details of easing curves.

You might also be interested in tests for your browser’s SVG implementation to see what is supported.

It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • Recent findings suggest that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

Recent findings suggest that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research reveals that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

Recent findings suggest that if you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

Industry observers note that in other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

Self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

Sources indicate that as you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

It has been revealed that when my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

Sources indicate that it can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Industry observers note that self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

To learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Fresh York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • It has been revealed that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Fresh York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Fresh York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in Upcoming York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

It has been revealed that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Fresh York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s unveiled that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

Sources indicate that the top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Industry observers note that mary Cassatt also established a fresh auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Sources indicate that only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

What Science Reveals About Gratitude’s Impact on the Brain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health.
  • Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion.
  • Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health. But very little is known about what actually happens in our brain and body when we experience it.

Why does that matter? Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion. The goal of my research has been to lay the groundwork for understanding what happens in the brain when we feel grateful—and a picture of the grateful brain is now starting to emerge.

Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.

When I first embarked on the journey to study gratitude, I came across philosophical treatises and religious exhortations emphasizing the importance of gratitude, along with scientific studies suggesting that gratitude can improve your sleep, enhance your romantic relationships, protect you from illness, motivate you to exercise, and boost your happiness, among many other benefits.

According to recent reports, at the time, however, very little was known about what happens in our brains and bodies when we experience gratitude, which made it difficult to understand how gratitude actually works. Since I’m a neuroscientist, I zeroed in on the neurobiology of gratitude with a more specific question in mind: Can our brain activity reveal anything about how gratitude achieves its significant benefits?

Recent findings suggest that given the clear relationship between mental and physical health, I thought that understanding what happens in the brain when we feel gratitude could tell us more about the mind-body connection—namely, how feeling positive emotion can improve bodily functions. I also thought these results could help scientists design programs aimed at generating gratitude by helping them zero in on the precise activities and experiences most essential to reaping gratitude’s benefits.

It must be mentioned that actually capturing people in the moment of feeling gratitude poses some challenges. After all, some people may not feel gratitude when we expect them to, and others may even feel grateful in unexpected situations. I thought my best bet would be to try to induce gratitude through powerful stories of aid and sacrifice.

To achieve this, I turned to the USC Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History, which houses the world’s largest repository of videotaped Holocaust survivor testimonies—many of which, perhaps surprisingly, are filled with breathtaking acts of selflessness and generosity. Along with a team of amazing undergraduates, I began by watching hundreds of hours of survivor testimony to find stories in which the survivor received help of some kind from another person.

We assembled a collection of these stories and transformed them into short scenarios that we shared with our participants. Each scenario was re-phrased into the second-person (e.g., “You are on a wintertime death march and a fellow prisoner gives you a warm coat”) and presented to our study’s participants. We asked them to imagine themselves in the scenario and feel, as much as possible, how they would feel if they were in the same situation. While participants reflected on these gifts, we measured their brain activity using modern brain imaging techniques (in the form of functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI).

The regions associated with gratitude are part of the neural networks that light up when we socialize and experience pleasure.

In a recent development, for each of these scenarios, we asked participants how much gratitude they felt, and we correlated this rating with their brain activity in that moment. While such an approach will not elicit exactly the same feelings as actually living through such situations, participants overwhelmingly reported strong feelings of gratitude, deep engagement in the task, and, perhaps even more importantly, an increased empathy for and understanding of the Holocaust as a result of participating in the study.

According to recent reports, what’s more, our results revealed that when participants reported those grateful feelings, their brains demonstrated activity in a set of regions located in the medial pre-frontal cortex, an area in the frontal lobes of the brain where the two hemispheres meet. This area of the brain is associated with understanding other people’s perspectives, empathy, and feelings of relief. This is also an area of the brain that is massively connected to the systems in the body and brain that regulate emotion and support the process of stress relief.

These data told us a reasonable story about gratitude:.

Industry observers note that glenn Fox, PhD, is a research fellow at USC’s Brain and Creativity Institute. He earned his PhD from the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of Southern California working with Antonio Damasio. His research focuses on social cognition, affective neuroscience and social influence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

According to recent reports, the reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the newly introduced government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are looks afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an crucial moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

In a recent development, according to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

It has been revealed that A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been declared. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has announced that a latest museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

It has been revealed that al-Dakhili has also unveiled that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement says.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.
  • It has been revealed that the first thing you see is the space between the letters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

It has been revealed that the first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

According to recent reports, the type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

The old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The latest system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

In a recent development, colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

According to recent reports, the system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor initiative layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

We simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

He garnered a lot of recognition for his work during the early 20th century and his nickname was “Champ,” and that is from where the hotel took its name.

Artists should receive tax breaks for donating their own work to UK museums, claims newly introduced philanthropy report

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a newly introduced report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.
  • The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.
  • The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a newly introduced report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

In a recent development, artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, claims the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

According to recent reports, charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he claims. “The biggest concern seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

The CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report says.

Industry observers note that UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, indicates: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

According to recent reports, “Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

In a recent development, the market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

Sources indicate that the brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a major serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

Industry observers note that we fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

The first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

Sources indicate that we used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

The tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

According to recent reports, the photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a upcoming one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

Sources indicate that with Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

According to recent reports, collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

As a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

According to recent reports, the Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has unveiled that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he mentioned he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has unveiled that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he mentioned he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

Industry observers note that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

In a recent development, but Gruijthuijsen stated he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he notes. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental shows of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he claims.

From the Finns, he will also bring an crucial lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he indicates: “Less talking, more doing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the fresh Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.
  • It has been revealed that co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative.
  • Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the fresh Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.

It has been revealed that co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative. Nearly 2,400 stores and more than five million members later, that fact still sets it apart, and SomeOne built the whole Brandworld on it. Under creative director Shaun Turnbull, the studio took the cloverleaf Co-op had brought back eight years before and broke it into five pieces, the Membershapes. Each piece is one of the mark's most recognisable forms, strong enough to stand alone, and together they carry the idea that every member owns a piece of Co-op. The shapes work as windows, holding devices, patterns and graphic devices, so the same blue field can hold a billboard headline, a phone screen price or a tote bag pattern, and the system still reads as one brand across Food, Funeralcare, Insurance and Legal Services.

The type does the shouting. Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol. The squircle-like corners and angled cuts on the c and p come straight from the mark, and the face is built to run in caps, loud and straight. SomeOne also made a textured version, an SVG cut with an ink-rolled texture created at St Bride Library in London, so the letters keep the uneven bite of letterpress blocks. The specimen sheet reveals the alphabet at full size, texture visible in every stroke, with the numbers set underneath in the same weight. On posters and app screens the type sits inside a Membershape, the shape doing the layout work while the caps do the talking.

The texture is the finish. That ink-rolled grain runs through the type, the shapes and the membership card, giving a national supermarket the feel of a printed pamphlet. History gets the same treatment: the old dividend stamps, the divi, return as a full sheet of blue stamps, each carrying the mark and a number, a direct line from 1844 to the present. Around it, the system stays practical. A lorry carries 'We're member driven' across a blue side panel, the app screens stack member prices and store finding under the same shapes, and the tote bag wears the Membershape pattern outright. An expressive icon set, drawn from the curves of the symbol, extends the language to every touchpoint, and the ambition is plain: grow membership from five million to eight million by 2030.

See more from SomeOne on their website.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently highlights:.

Industry observers note that the savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (Newly introduced York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

Recent findings suggest that one important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

Recent findings suggest that the old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

Industry observers note that what does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:.

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech company on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Sources indicate that fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the concern, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so upcoming. Striking the balance was critical.

Industry observers note that the result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

According to recent reports, the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

Industry observers note that WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

According to recent reports, an notable first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Recent findings suggest that inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

According to recent reports, our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

To further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

The brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

Sources indicate that WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

Breaking: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar.
  • “At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, noted at the end of the evening.
  • Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, noted at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Industry observers note that the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

In a recent development, A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

In a recent development, A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Among the night’s other massive-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Industry observers note that J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Industry observers note that arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).
