📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.
  • Recent findings suggest that the book reads as one long strip of history.
  • According to recent reports, the layout was not placed by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.

Recent findings suggest that the book reads as one long strip of history. More than 1,000 photographs, illustrations, and documents sit on a continuous timeline that runs from 1774 to 2024, and images cross the gutter from one page to the next so the story never breaks. A hundred historical events sit alongside the timeline, with notes on the social conditions of each era, and a 60-page index at the back sorts everything by model, country, and document type. What holds it together is restraint: the pages stay pale, the captions stay small, and the archive does the talking.

According to recent reports, the layout was not placed by hand. Bureau Borsche built the book from a dedicated online database of 2,500 archived objects, each tagged with year, type, category, location, and shoe model, and pulled the material through an API. Column widths, cropping, and DPI were decided by custom code and rendered in the browser with JavaScript, so the grid flexes around the material instead of forcing the material into a fixed frame.

Page numbers were placed automatically, and the index pages generated themselves from the same data, with references pointing back to the pages they came from. The final step exported every page as a single-page PDF. It is design systems thinking applied to a book: the rules are written once, and 608 pages follow them.

Three paper stocks divide the book into sections, and each one changes how the images sit. The archival section prints on yellow-tinted, semi-transparent paper, so the documents feel thin and handled. The middle section, photographs and advertisements, sits on glossy greyish stock. The final section moves to bright white glossy paper, the kind used for fashion magazines and art catalogs.

The cover keeps the same quiet register. It is blind-stamped on extra rough cardboard, carrying the first recorded mention of a Birkenstock shoemaker, from a church file dated 1774, with only the year printed in small black type at the centre. The spine does the loud work instead: the wordmark runs down it in heavy black capitals, with Steidl at the foot.

From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”.
  • Sources indicate that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up.
  • “A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” states the Latest York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

Sources indicate that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” states the Latest York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.

It has been revealed that certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

In a recent development, “There’s definitely a hierarchy,” indicates Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

Industry observers note that however, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, says Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in Fresh York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Recent findings suggest that besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

It has been revealed that other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” notes Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the Upcoming Britain Museum.

Recent findings suggest that N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth.

Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” notes Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Sources indicate that specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum indicates, and the Leyendecker is not right now “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”.

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

It has been revealed that most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

Recent findings suggest that here's the critical nuance that trips up newly introduced consumers: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.

The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Recent findings suggest that the painting, made around 1662 by an unknown artist, gives a bird’s-eye view of the house and Italian-style gardens at Llannerch Park which “contained a series of marvellous watery innovations: pools, fountains, sculpture, cascades and hydraulic surprises all set off by Baroque architecture, staircases and planting”, says Pippa Shirley, a member of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art and objects of cultural interest which advises the government. The fact that the garden is now lost makes the painting more key, she adds in a statement.

Sources indicate that the Llannerch Park garden was created by the landowner Mutton Davies following a tour of France and Italy; according to Sotheby’s, which offered the painting in a sale in 2014 in London, Davies also commissioned the landscape painting in the 1660s, and had remained in the family since. The work failed to sell at the 2014 auction, where it was estimated to sell at £400,000-£600,000. A government spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the painting's ownership. A slightly smaller version of the painting is housed at the Yale Center for British Art in Connecticut.

“If the painting remains in the UK, researchers will be given the opportunity to explore how people and culture were spreading between Wales, England and the European continent in the seventeenth century. It could also reveal latest details about how the artistry of country-estate landscapes developed in Britain,” according to the UK Department for Digital, Media, Culture and Sport.

#126045. Fatbergs, pigeons and Pankhurst: rebranded London Museum opens newly introduced £437m home

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (802 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Fatbergs, pigeons and Pankhurst: rebranded London Museum opens newly introduced £437m home

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The newly introduced London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.
  • Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum.
  • According to recent reports, based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The newly introduced London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.

Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum.

According to recent reports, based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London. The new complex, one of Europe’s largest cultural infrastructure projects, is designed by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan in partnership with the conservation architects Julian Harrap.

Industry observers note that the museum caused a stir in 2024 when it unveiled a rebrand centred around the image of a defecating pigeon. Sharon Ament, the museum director, tells The Art Newspaper: “It’s not often a museum brand gets into the news. I think that’s because people saw, in our pigeon, the city and their experience: a place full of contrasts. It’s beautiful, it’s fun, it’s also a bit scruffy! I don’t think there’s a better representation of us than a pigeon.”.

The first phase of the London Museum will open in a Victorian part of the Smithfield Market © Secchi Smith.

The new museum site will open in two phases: the formerly derelict Victorian General Market dating from the 1880s, home to the permanent galleries, will open on 28 November, while the 1960s Poultry Market, which houses a learning centre, temporary exhibition spaces and on-site interactive collection store, will launch in 2028.

“We are using time as an organising principle, so our major spaces all behave differently with their own emphasis, objects and vibe,” says Ament. The General Market houses the Past Time and Our Time sections, plus Night Time. Past Time spans 2,000 years, telling the story of London via landmark events like the Great Fire in 1666 and the 2012 Olympics.

A chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg © London Museum.

“Stars of the collection” like the Cheapside Hoard of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewels; the medal given to Pankhurst to commemorate her 1912 hunger strike; and a sample of the fatberg—a 250-metre long mass of oil and wet wipes—will also feature in Past Time.

It has been revealed that “We have two significant but very contrasting buildings in the Victorian General Market and the listed 1960s Poultry Market, representing different moments in London’s history. We think about them as two of the biggest objects in our collection and they lend themselves to different experiences,” claims Ament.

In a recent development, our Time in the Linbury Hall is a social hub at the heart of London Museum, set across the former trading floor of the General Market. Around its perimeter, a restaurant, shop and show space for families and schools sits alongside 13 large installations exploring the ways Londoners have come together © Hufton + Crow.

Asked if the museum is just for Londoners, she notes that the city’s residents will discover newly introduced stories from the city’s vast history, and be part of telling its story today, while for international visitors, “this is a great first place to start their immersion in London”. The museum has an ambitious visitor figure target of over two million annually.

In a recent development, there are 18 people in the curatorial team but the museum is also supported by an academic advisory panel and “some 100,000 people from London and beyond” who have helped shaped the museum. These include various focus groups, community and school groups, and advisory panels such as the museum’s Access Panel and Family Panel.

View into part of London Museum’s "London Tastes" display, exploring the changing appetites of a global food city © Hufton + Crow.

In a recent development, the cost of the newly introduced museum has risen to £437m in total (the budget was set at £337m in 2019). The Greater London Authority, under mayor Sadiq Khan, has given £95m, while the City of London Corporation is contributing £222m. A range of private foundations and sponsors including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Goldsmiths’ Foundation, the Linbury Trust and the National Lottery Heritage Fund are also backing the project.

As for running costs, statutory funding comes from the City of London Corporation and the Mayor of London, Ament states.

“We also want to find ways to stand on our own feet more,” she notes. “That means support from commercial partnerships and activities, like retail, ticket sales, our ‘fan club’ [the museum’s membership] and venue hire. We’re also leasing spaces, known as the museum ‘Houses’, that sit around the perimeter of the General Market, so now we are landlords as well.” She says the sites are sustainable through the use of solar panels and smart technology.

#126039. Munch museum appoints Thorsten Sadowsky as upcoming director

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (714 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Munch museum appoints Thorsten Sadowsky as upcoming director

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director.
  • Sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions.
  • “My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director. Sadowsky, who joins Munch from Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf) in northern Germany, will begin his new role on 1 May 2027.

Sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions. His current position involves the management of multiple museums in the Schleswig-Holstein area, including the Museum of Art and Cultural History Schloss Gottorf and the Jewish Museum Rendsburg. Previously he has also directed the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum and the Kirchner Museum Davos, which is focused on the life and career of the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.

“My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper. “Such a museum offers an exceptional opportunity to engage with an artist’s oeuvre with a degree of intensity and depth that is rarely possible in an art museum with a more broadly based collection. The challenge, however, is to ensure that the focus on a single artist does not lead to intellectual or curatorial narrowness.”.

Sadowsky adds that his task is therefore “to continually open up new perspectives, reveal unexpected connections and bring the artist’s work into dialogue with other artistic practices, historical experiences and contemporary concerns”.

Sources indicate that the Munch museum, which opened in a sprawling upcoming home on Oslo’s Bjørvika waterfront in 2021, houses nearly 27,000 works of art by Munch. Alongside its permanent displays, the museum hosts a temporary exhibition programme that has brought Munch’s work into dialogue with that of contemporary artists such as Tracey Emin, Katherina Grosse and Alice Neel, as well as events such as concerts and conferences. It has welcome more than 700,000 visitors so far this year, according to a release.

In a recent development, sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper that he first encountered Munch’s work at the Hamburger Kunsthaller, while he was a university student. The opportunity to direct the museum, he says, is exciting thanks to "the extraordinary richness of [Munch’s] artistic legacy. Beyond the familiar image of Munch as a painter of anxiety, loneliness and existential uncertainty, there is still much to discover. His work speaks equally of vitality, human relationships, our experience of nature and the social transformations of modernity.“.

“Few artists have succeeded so convincingly in transforming individual experiences into images of universal human significance,” he adds. “In the realm of sculpture, Alberto Giacometti is another artist who achieved something similar.”.

In his previous role as director of the Museum der Modern Salzburg, Sadowsky spoke about the importance of widening the scope of the programme and collection. He told the Austrian art magazine Parnass in 2022: “During my tenure as director, a major focus has been on broadening our perspective beyond the Western European canon and incorporating more postcolonial viewpoints.”.

Recent findings suggest that in his new role, Sadowsky claims his immediate priority will be to “listen, to learn and to develop and deeper understanding“ of the institution and its people. “Over the coming years, I would like to further strengthen the Munch Museum as the world’s foremost centre of expertise on Edvard Munch, while continuing to develop it as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution,” he adds.

The Munch museum is owned by the city of Oslo. Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s vice mayor for culture and business development, notes in a statement: “I am delighted that Munch [museum] will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts. Sadowsky has headed several highly respected art museums and has demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading Munch [museum] into the future.”.

Sources indicate that sadowsky takes over from Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed in October. Hansen left to lead Moderna Museet in Stockholm.

The Munch museum directorship runs as a six-year term, with the potential for one renewal.

#126034. Porto Rocha Unveils the Kunsthalle Basel identity

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (425 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abduzeedo ↗ Open Full Page

Porto Rocha Unveils the Kunsthalle Basel identity

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Porto Rocha rebuilt the Kunsthalle Basel identity around one stretchable KB monogram, a custom serif, and color that finally indicates up.
  • Kunsthalle Basel has spent 150 years showing artists before anyone else caught on, from Marcel Duchamp to Anne Imhof, with no permanent collection and a habit of betting on what comes next.
  • Industry observers note that type does the talking once the mark steps back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Porto Rocha rebuilt the Kunsthalle Basel identity around one stretchable KB monogram, a custom serif, and color that finally indicates up.

Kunsthalle Basel has spent 150 years showing artists before anyone else caught on, from Marcel Duchamp to Anne Imhof, with no permanent collection and a habit of betting on what comes next. Its old identity could not carry that energy. Director Mohamed Almusibli arrived in 2024 wanting the institution to act as a true host, warm and open to anyone curious enough to walk in, and Porto Rocha answered with what the studio calls an institutional brand with an anti-institutional spirit. Everything hangs on one mark. The K and B merge into a single gesture that reads as either letter, a confident stamp when it sits still and a shape that stretches, compresses and rotates when the context asks it to.

Industry observers note that type does the talking once the mark steps back. Porto Rocha worked with Swiss foundry Maxitype on KB Rhymes, a custom headline serif with roots in Times New Roman, humanist in feel and slightly condensed so it holds its own at large sizes without shouting over the art. Suisse International handles body copy and exhibition text, plain and highly legible. The specimen page sets artist names in KB Rhymes at poster scale, white on black, and the letters carry the same soft serifs and generous curves as the monogram. Behind the mark, a construction grid pins the K inside an oval, with guide lines marking the geometry that keeps the stretched and rotated versions honest.

In a recent development, the system earns its keep on the small things. A stack of cards carries the K at full bleed, black on white. A flat lay of programs, posters, a keyring and a lighter demonstrates the mark in a dozen colors at once, from a pink oval to a blue Werkstatt Sessions cover. The matchbox is the best of the bunch, a black box with a white K that slides open on purple-tipped matches.

Out on the street, the Opening Night poster frames a blue K oval on the stone facade, and a brushed metal plaque sets the orange mark under silver Kunsthalle Basel lettering. In the galleries, the identity steps aside and lets the work and the neoclassical rooms do the talking, which is the point. Two color modes run through it all, neutral beside artwork and loud in type-led layouts, where the old identity avoided color altogether.

See more from Porto Rocha on their website.

The eighth edition of Frieze Los Angeles will welcome 102 exhibitors under the sprawling white tent on the grounds of the Santa Monica Airport. The exhibitor list, as in previous years, includes heavy local representation—with more than one-third of participants operating a space in Los Angeles.

The roster includes established Los Angeles galleries such as Jeffrey Deitch, Regen Projects, David Kordansky, Château Shatto, Commonwealth and Council, Anat Ebgi, Night Gallery, the Pit and Roberts Projects. Four younger Los Angeles galleries will make their debuts in the Focus section for emerging galleries: Megan Mulrooney, Rajiv Menon Contemporary, House of Seiko and Zodiac Pictures. Erin Christovale from the Hammer Museum will curate this section.

According to recent reports, international blue-chip galleries returning to Frieze Los Angeles include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Pace, White Cube, Perrotin, Gladstone, Almine Rech, Thaddaeus Ropac and Sprüth Magers. First-time exhibitors include Gallery Wendi Norris from San Francisco, Franklin Parrasch in New York, G Gallery in Seoul, Newchild in Antwerp, and Yehudi Hollander-Pappi and Danielian in Brazil.

A handful of prominent galleries will not be returning after taking part in recent editions, like Berggruen Gallery from San Francisco, Ortuzar and Tina Kim Gallery in Fresh York, Mendes Wood DM and Nara Roesler from Brazil, Southern Guild from Cape Town and Timothy Taylor from London. Turnover year-over-year remains around 28% for a second consecutive year, amid stable overall exhibitor numbers.

Visitors to the fair will be greeted at the entrance by a latest work by the Los Angeles-based artist rafa esparza called Queercancha, painted across two adobe panels mounted on chrome steel, drawing on Southern California’s culture of lowrider cruising.

Amid a boom following the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, art dealers from all over the world began setting up shop in the Los Angeles area. However, many of those outposts have since closed alongside local dealerships—most recently, the Landing on Jefferson Boulevard. Along with a global market downturn, many local businesses were hurt by the devastating 2025 wildfires that nearly saw that year’s edition of Frieze Los Angeles cancelled. A handful of galleries have closed their local spaces and shifted their attentions to Latest York, including Southern Guild and Pietro Alexander.

This may be one of the final years the fair will be held at the Santa Monica Airport; the facility is scheduled to close permanently to aviation at the end of 2028 for conversion into a public park.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TIME has released its annual Top 100 Photos of the Year feature, celebrating striking images that capture the biggest moments and events of 2026. One of the featured photos was shot by acclaimed photographer and filmmaker Jimmy Chin using the iPhone 18 Pro, marking a milestone for Apple’s latest flagship smartphone and, of course, Chin himself.

Chin, an Academy Award-winning director, National Geographic photographer, and accomplished mountaineer, photographed his longtime climbing partner, Conrad Anker, as part of a fresh series, What Holds Us. Chin and Anker have climbed together for 25 years, scaling peaks around the world.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.

“Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture.”.

For Chin, who has shot in many extreme and remote locations throughout his career, the smaller and lighter the gear, the better.

Sources indicate that “A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame,” Chin continues.

Using Apple’s upcoming iPhone 18 Pro, Chin was able to travel lighter without sacrificing performance or image quality. As his photo above demonstrates, the iPhone 18 Pro more than delivered — a testament to just how far smartphone imaging technology has come. Chin is far from the only photographer or filmmaker to integrate an iPhone into a professional workflow in recent years.

Chin shot 48MP ProRAW photos the iPhone 18 Pro and then stitched multiple shots to create one of his signature panoramas. The final photo is over 300 megapixels and 25,000 pixels wide. There’s no question it holds up extremely well in the large print featured in the What Holds Us exhibit.

According to recent reports, chin’s photos are also part of the What Holds Us exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, appearing alongside works by Alex Prager and Jack Davison. After debuting in New York City in September, the exhibition opens in London on December 4, running at Saatchi Yates Gallery through December 13.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has revealed the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.
  • Sources indicate that deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor.
  • British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has revealed the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.

Sources indicate that deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor. Widely regarded as one of the greatest cinematographers in film history, Deakins has won two Academy Awards for Best Cinematography and five BAFTA Awards in the same category.

British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30). At the beginning of his career, Benson was already attracting significant national and international recognition. His work spans documentary photography, choreography, and abstraction, exploring the nature of photography and its relationship with contemporary life.

Sources indicate that the RPS Progress Medal in the Science of Photography has been awarded to Professor Marc Levoy, an American computer graphics researcher and Professor Emeritus of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. Levoy is also a vice president and fellow at Adobe and a Distinguished Engineer at Google.

According to recent reports, british photographic artist Mandy Barker is the recipient of The RPS Award for Environmental Responsibility. Barker is internationally recognized for her work documenting marine plastic debris. Working alongside scientists, she uses photography to highlight the scale of plastic pollution in the world’s oceans and its impact on marine life and the wider environment.

It has been revealed that documentary photographer and filmmaker Polly Braden has received the RPS Award for Social Impact. Her long-term collaborative projects explore how people live and work, and their place in society. Her latest project, Against the Tide, produced with The Guardian, followed young people in 17 coastal towns. The project was exhibited at Arnolfini in Bristol and Firstsite in Colchester, and also brought 16 young people to Parliament to give evidence to MPs.

Now in its 148th year, the Royal Photographic Society Awards date back to 1878. The Society describes them as the world’s longest-running photography awards. They recognize achievements across still and moving images, celebrating individuals rather than individual photographs. The awards cover a broad range of disciplines, including moving image, upcoming media, science and imaging, education, publishing, and curation.

Victoria Humphries, CEO of the Royal Photographic Society, says the awards reflect the breadth of the photographic community and the many ways people contribute to the medium.

“The RPS Awards provide an opportunity to recognize and celebrate those who are making a difference, whether through their creativity, innovation, research, education or their contribution to the wider photographic community,” Humphries states.

“As an organization, we believe that photography is for everyone, and these RPS Awards demonstrate that there are so many different ways to engage with, contribute to and shape its future.”.

Deakins states he is particularly pleased to be recognized for his still photography, given his career in cinematography.

According to recent reports, “I’m very honored to receive this award from the Royal Photographic Society. Although I have been more known for my work in cinematography, still photography has always been a passion and more personal to me. To be recognized by the Royal Photographic Society for my work in stills is amazing and means a great deal to me.”.

The complete list of RPS 2026 Awards Recipients is available here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The charity Art Explora has revealed the five winners of the 2026 edition of its Académie des beaux-arts European Award, which recognises innovative work by non-profit arts and culture organisations in Europe. They are Polish performing arts foundation Jazdaa Polska!, Spanish art and health organisation Cultura en Vena, the French library charity Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, UK literary organisation London Writers Centre and Slovakian theatre organization RAMAGU. The organisations were awarded funds ranging from €30,000-50,000, shared from a total £180,000.

The winners were revealed at an award ceremony at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London on the evening of 24 November. Each of them, apart from RAMAGU—which won an audience choice award—was selected by an international jury, which included several members of the Académie des beaux-arts in Paris, such as the illustrator Emmanuel Guibert and the sculptor Eva Jospin; Vanja Kaludjercic, the director of the International Film Festival Rotterdam; and Antonija Letinić, a cultural development consultant in Croatia. Frédéric Jousset, the French entrepreneur and founder of Art Explora, was also a juror.

Cultura en Vena, who has been awarded €40,000, will puts the funds towards its Arte Ambulatorio project, which brings reproductions of works of art and other forms of creative programming into hospital spaces. The new phase of the project will involve an exhibition inspired by the work of Frida Kahlo, as well as live music sessions and creative writing workshops for children. Previous Arte Ambulatorio interventions focused on the work of the Spanish artists Francisco Goya and Joaquín Sorolla.

According to the organisation, “Frida Kahlo’s artistic universe offers a powerful entry point into themes closely connected to the hospital experience: the body, pain, vulnerability, identity, resilience, emotional expression and care.”.

Industry observers note that “Cultura en Vena takes art as seriously as care,” Jousset tells The Art Newspaper. He notes the jury was convinced by “their rigour”. “They measure their impact and keep improving each exhibition based on patients’ and staff feedback,” he continues. “With over 23,000 peopkeople reached last year, they are one of the leading voices in arts and wellbeing in Spain.”.

Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, meanwhile, will put its €50,000 award towards its L’autre retour project. The initiative involves workshops within which Ukrainian veterans are invited to draw, read and write with members of their community outside of a clinical environment, in an effort to help with reintegration after the military. The charity then plans to tour some of the works in Ukraine, as well as show them at the European Commission in Brussels.

“This project shows art as an act of rebuilding,” Jousset indicates.

The additional funded projects include developing touch-based choreography with blind and partially-sighted people in Poland (Jazdaa Polska!), making Lewisham in London the UK’s first “Borough of Literature” (London Writers Centre), and creating documentary theatre with minority groups in rural Slovakia (RAMAGU).

Tech Report: Rare 1889 Photo of Historic Newly introduced York Giants Baseball Team Is Up for Auction

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare cabinet photograph of the Fresh York Giants, one of early professional baseball’s most significant teams, taken by renowned baseball photographer Joseph Hall in 1889, is up for auction.
  • One of Major League Baseball’s oldest franchises, the Newly introduced York Giants rose to prominence in the late 19th century, winning back-to-back championships in 1888 and 1889, before the modern World Series was established in 1903.
  • According to recent reports, the photograph, which is being offered by auction house Huggins & Scott as part of a sale which runs through December 3, features the New York Giants team that won the 1888 World Championship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare cabinet photograph of the Fresh York Giants, one of early professional baseball’s most significant teams, taken by renowned baseball photographer Joseph Hall in 1889, is up for auction.

One of Major League Baseball’s oldest franchises, the Newly introduced York Giants rose to prominence in the late 19th century, winning back-to-back championships in 1888 and 1889, before the modern World Series was established in 1903. The team boasted several future Baseball Hall of Famers during this era. Its legacy continues today as the San Francisco Giants, following the franchise’s relocation from New York to California in 1958.

According to recent reports, the photograph, which is being offered by auction house Huggins & Scott as part of a sale which runs through December 3, features the New York Giants team that won the 1888 World Championship. The auction house claims it has never handled another example of this particular photograph in its imperial cabinet format, making it one of the rarest of Joseph Hall’s baseball team photographs.

Industry observers note that hall photographed many of the Major League baseball teams in 1888 and was widely regarded as the leading baseball photographer of the late 1880s. Hall’s cabinet photographs of professional baseball teams and players are among the most sought-after photographic collectibles of the late 19th century, with his images of teams posing in uniform at ballparks commanding the highest prices.

According to recent reports, while a smaller cabinet card featuring the same image of the Giants appeared at auction several years ago, Huggins & Scott indicates it cannot recall seeing another example of this photograph in this larger format. According to the auction house, the size and quality of the print are particularly noteworthy given the limitations of photographic production in the late 19th century. Producing photographs of this scale and quality required a considerable investment of time and resources, and the auction house suggests that only a small number of prints may have been made.

According to recent reports, unlike other photographs Hall took of the Giants that feature an outdoor stadium background, the image highlights 19 members of the team posing together in a studio. Among those pictured are six future Baseball Hall of Famers: Tim Keefe, Roger Connor, Buck Ewing, Jim O’Rourke, John Montgomery Ward, and Mickey Welch.

The photograph is up for sale in the Fall Auction at Huggins & Scott Auctions, which runs through December 3.

Upcoming York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features.
  • As The Verge reports, The Latest York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.
  • The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to customers.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features. Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.

As The Verge reports, The Latest York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to customers.”.

The Times‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself. Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand. The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.

Sources indicate that new York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos. In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events. This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed. It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene. Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.

Recent findings suggest that the Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers. The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.

It has been revealed that what has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata. This appears to be the primary concern for The New York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.

According to recent reports, “It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software. At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this newly introduced version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

Recent findings suggest that to prevent these issues, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times—an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers. Fortunately, it is possible for owners to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward. As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

Adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community. The Times‘s new policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.

PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication. This story will be updated with any response.

  • The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M.
  • According to recent reports, the images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.

The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M. EST on November 9. This was approximately three hours after the spacecraft made its closest approach to Earth, when it was about 38,500 miles away and had a clear view of the Western Hemisphere.

According to recent reports, the images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month. Both spacecraft used a combination of engine burns and Earth’s gravity to gain momentum for their 10-month journey to Mars.

Once they reach orbit around the Red Planet, the spacecraft will study how the solar wind — a stream of charged particles traveling at around a million miles per hour from the Sun — interacts with Mars’ environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

A commercial satellite captured images of the pair from approximately 3,000 miles away, while a member of the mission team photographed the spacecraft passing overhead from his home near Los Angeles (below).

It has been revealed that two spacecraft. Two flybys. One path to Mars.

Photographed from the Los Angeles area, Blue and Gold streaked through the same part of the sky two days apart—Blue in blue, Gold in gold. https://t.co/9SDOMmqqtY.

— Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 23, 2026.

Industry observers note that NASA explains that the ESCAPADE mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division and is part of the agency’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission, working with partners including Rocket Lab, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space, and Blue Origin.

Grand Theft Auto VI takes over Miami, including its art destinations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.
  • According to recent reports, on 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property.
  • The art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.

According to recent reports, on 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property. The museum also declared the partnership would include merchandising and free admission for all Miami-Dade County residents until the end of 2028, reversing a pandemic-era policy that saw tickets sold at the attraction for the first time.

The art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim. Set in a satirical version of Miami called “Vice City”, the game world is an incredibly detailed virtual replica of the real city and the surrounding state of Florida (“Leonida”), complete with areas such as “Stockyard” replicating Wynwood with its street art and graffiti culture.

Sources indicate that art galleries in the digital replica of Wynwood (the "Stockyard" neighbourhood) inside Grand Theft Auto VI Screenshot by The Art Newspaper. Courtesy Rockstar Games.

Demonstrating an extreme dedication to realism, Rockstar has even painstakingly replicated and renamed local landmarks such as the nightclub Club Space (“The Vault”), the beloved regional casual dining chain Flanigan’s (“Uncle Jack’s) and local art institutions such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami ("Future Leonida Art Museum", or "Flam") and the Wolfsonian–Florida International University design museum ("Hicksonian Museum of Art and Design"). Miami Beach’s Bass Museum of Art (“Vice City Museum of Art”) had its iconic Ugo Rondinone sculpture Miami Mountain (2016) turned into a monumental stack of emojis inside the game. (Unfortunately the current exhibition at the "Vice City Museum of Art", Karl Bergstrom: Diaspora, cannot be visited as the building is not currently accessible within gameplay.).

It has been revealed that according to Jessica Goldman Srebnick, the Wynwood Walls museum’s chief executive and curator, Rockstar commissioned in-game murals from around 50 artists, many of whom have exhibited at the museum before. When the developer approached the museum to suggest a collaboration, it was a no-brainer. “Street art and gaming have a lot of shared cultural DNA, and they’ve influenced each other,” she says. The game’s creators “share our commitment to creativity, to supporting artists. They share our commitment and deep appreciation for the city of Miami. And I’m just really grateful that they are supporting something that provides more access to the arts.”.

A Grand Theft Auto VI-themed mural by Queen Andrea in the real Wynwood neighbourhood of Miami Courtesy Queen Andrea and Wynwood Walls Museum.

Industry observers note that the murals in Wynwood, which will be on display until 1 January 2027, are similar to those featured in the game itself. A mural by the artist Queen Andrea, for instance, reads “Welcome to Vice City” in a curvy, neon-like font, while another by Ron English features a design with grenades in the shape of lightbulbs and the slogan: “There’s nothing more dangerous than a good idea.”.

In a recent development, the project, as well as GTA’s larger presence in the city, has not been without controversy. The local newspaper Miami Upcoming Times reported on 10 November that one of the GTA murals had covered up a piece by the late artist Alex “Rect” Reyes, who finished the work shortly before his death in 2022. The wall had been considered a memorial by Reyes’s family and friends, who say they were not informed about its replacement. Goldman Global Arts, which owns the wall and museum, said in a statement to the New Times that it had offered Reyes’s crew a different wall to make amends.

The digital replica of Miami Beach's Bass Museum of Art within Grand Theft Auto VI, the "Vice City Museum of Art", with an emoji-themed parody of its Ugo Rondinone public sculpture Image courtesy of IGN / Official Grand Theft Auto VI Strategy Guide.

Meanwhile, a joint partnership with Miami-Dade County and the Miami Heat professional basketball team has resulted in everything from player uniforms to the Kaseya Center arena in Downtown Miami being rebranded with “Vice City”. Massive crowds turned out for a Heat game on 18 November, the eve of the GTA VI’s release, to purchase custom merchandise that was only available at the arena. The total package, which includes lighting and signage inspired by the game at Miami International Airport and PortMiami, is valued at $3.9m according to a press release from the county government. Some officials have expressed alarm at the collaboration, with one county commissioner worried that the game is “depicting Miami like a murder capital”, according to the Miami Herald.

As for the benefits for the local art scene, perhaps gamers who visit GTA VI’s virtual “Vice City Museum of Art” will be inspired to seek out the Bass on their next visit to Miami Beach.

Because the full name is long, Fix Studio condensed it into an acronym built from FK Roman Standard and paired it with FK Grotesk Neue. In a recent development, at launch, IOC didnât have a cohort yet, so photography came mostly from Gregory-Riveraâs own archive. Type had to carry the room. Borrowing the resourceful logic of typewriter-era concrete poetry, Fix Studio broke lines out of rigid columns so words drift across the page. On the framed off-white poster, small FK Roman Standard lines scatter across open space to map the Caribbean archipelago, a gesture the website repeats on scroll. Inside a Documento Alterno spread, grey serif words tumble diagonally down a charcoal page opposite Adriana Moreiraâs photo essay, while a sage-green street poster staggers FK Grotesk Neue above candid Puerto Rican photography. Color stays disciplined across the visual identity â mostly off-white and off-black, keeping pastel green, blue, yellow, and red for accents or Spanish and English social posts.

In a recent development, to keep that drift grounded, Fix Studio built a quiet counterweight drawn from archival indexing. Stepped horizontal rules nest category labels inside one another across website navigation, poster headers like Presenta / ExhibiciÃ³n, and the Documento Alterno Vol 02 cover pairing bilingual Ciclo / Cycle 2026 type with a flowering plant pushing through concrete. This visual identity isnât frozen in a binder. Torres Viera calls it a system in motion that will keep adapting as future fellowship cycles turn IOCâs imagery into a rotating photographic archive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filmmakers will soon be able to get their hands on the large-format Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 cinema camera for considerably less money than before.

As NewsShooter reports, a “body-only” version of the GFX Eterna 55 has appeared for preorder at some retailers, including B&H. It costs $9,999, compared to $16,499 for the standard GFX Eterna 55 package.

Saving $6,500 is significant, so what does that extra money actually get video creators?

It has been revealed that the standard GFX Eterna 55 includes a custom 5-inch external touchscreen monitor with a mount and hood, a dedicated top handle with customizable controls, and AC power cables. Whether that bundle is worth $6,500 will depend on the individual user, of course.

PetaPixel YouTube host Dmitry Koshutin has used the GFX Eterna 55 extensively and believes the top handle is arguably the camera’s best feature.

According to recent reports, “The top handle is probably the best feature of the Eterna,” Koshutin states. “It’s very sturdy, and the controls are very handy. I would still want that, knowing how well it’s built.”.

As of yet, the GFX Eterna 55’s dedicated top handle is not listed as an optional accessory or available for separate purchase. At least for now, the only way for filmmakers to get it is by buying the standard GFX Eterna 55 kit for $16,499.

Recent findings suggest that koshutin is also a fan of the Eterna’s included external monitor, especially for filming fast-paced action, noting that its proprietary connection works very well. However, he adds that third-party monitors using SDI or HDMI can also be strong alternatives, offering larger or brighter displays.

Sources indicate that “Having stated that, $10,000 is quite a deal,” Koshutin concludes. “For filmmakers who already own top handle accessories and a monitor, shaving that extra $6,500 off makes a lot of sense without losing much functionality.”.

The Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 (Body Only) is available for preorder now at $9,999. It is also listed on Fujifilm’s own store, though it is marked “out of stock” and not yet available for preorder there. B&H right now lists the body-only GFX Eterna 55 as “coming soon.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, has been out in the wild for a month now, and more apps are being updated to natively support the dual-screened device all the time. Adobe Lightroom just got a major iPhone Duo compatibility update this week, and it is a strong example of how good the Duo can be.

As Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom Product Designer, Johannes Eckert, explains on Threads, the Adobe team has worked hard to fully optimize Lightroom for Duo.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo version of Lightroom works as normal on the device’s front screen, but when opened up, it is an entirely transformed experience, showing photos much larger than on other iPhone models and moving editing tools to the side. There’s also a “laptop pose,” as Eckert claims, that puts editing tools on the bottom while the photo stays above the fold.

In PetaPixel‘s testing, the updated app worked as promised and delivered a genuinely pleasant mobile photo editing experience. It’s nice to see my photos on the Duo’s large internal screen and to be able to access sliders, presets, masking tools, and more without obscuring my photo at all or needing to shrink it way down. You can still actually see your photo while utilizing Lightroom’s suite of editing tools, which is a big improvement over a standard iPhone photo editing experience.

That mentioned, there is still some room for improvement, and it seems like Adobe is already working on making tweaks. For example, when doing a Curves edit, the curves themselves appear on as an overlay on the photo, which is fine, except that it leaves much of the Duo’s inner screen totally empty.

“I think it’s better to have the curves to [the] right to get rid of the empty space,” Threads user itsrongarcia commented on Eckert’s original post.

It has been revealed that “We agree. This will be in the next update!” Eckert replied.

It has been revealed that other customers are looking forward to Adobe bringing some of its more powerful editing tools over from iPad, arguing that Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip is more than capable of running things like automatic dust removal and AI-powered noise reduction. There’s no word yet on whether Adobe is considering these things at this time.

Adobe will no doubt refine the iPhone Duo version of Lightroom further as more real-world users get to test it out and offer their feedback, but so far, so good. Ultimately, the iPhone Duo’s lasting appeal will depend heavily on how apps utilize its distinct form factor. Lightroom is definitely taking full advantage of it, and Lightroom mobile has never been as enjoyable to use.

The Hedonistic Days of Raving in Europe Revealed in Newly introduced Photo Book

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.
  • Sources indicate that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004.
  • Recent findings suggest that rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.

Sources indicate that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004. The images document a period when free parties were spreading across Europe, offering an alternative to mainstream society through music, community, and a shared rejection of conventional lifestyles.

Recent findings suggest that rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture. Their photographs provide a firsthand account of a counterculture built around emotion, affection, and togetherness, at a time when music and personal connections — rather than social media and mass communication — brought people together.

The book spans 196 black-and-white pages and brings together previously unseen photographs that capture the atmosphere and values of the era. Its accompanying text is written by Tobia D’Onofrio, author of Rave Upcoming World, who explores the history and significance of the European free-party movement.

“Rave was born as a disappearing ritual in which the art of invisibility was practiced, and parties were temporarily autonomous and free zones that appeared and disappeared into thin air within a few hours,” says D’Onofrio.

“1997–2004 can therefore be considered the golden age of the so-called illegal free parties and of rave culture. It was the moment of the phenomenon’s expansion across Europe… the rave scene had been criminalized to the point that in 1994 the Criminal Justice Act in England outlawed free parties. At that point, the energies shifted to the rest of Europe, and Italy immediately became the scene of legendary parties.”.

Sources indicate that the book examines how rave culture developed into more than a musical movement. It represented a rejection of conventional working and social structures, embracing communal living, constant movement, and a different relationship with time and space. Free parties became meeting places for people united by anarchic sensibilities and a desire to escape everyday routines.

Clementi and Morandi both attended the same high school in Milan before pursuing separate careers. Despite taking different paths, both remained dedicated to photography, eventually bringing their shared rave-scene experiences together in Never Alone.

The book is available online and through specialist bookstores.

#126008. Thelma Golden will step down as leader of the Studio Museum in Harlem after 21 years

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1018 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Thelma Golden will step down as leader of the Studio Museum in Harlem after 21 years

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired.
  • It has been revealed that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s latest six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street.
  • “It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired. Announcing the impending leadership transition on Tuesday (24 November), Kathryn C. Chenault, the chair of the museum’s board, remarked Golden “is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a new generation she helped foster”.

It has been revealed that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s latest six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street. That project had been a focus of much of the past decade of her tenure, including helping to raise a total of $322m as part of a capital campaign supporting construction and growing the museum’s endowment from $5m to $95m. The museum now has significantly more public areas; more galleries for special exhibitions and displays of its public collection; more centrally located studios for its residency programme; a rooftop terrace; and a number of key front- and back-of-house amenities it previously lacked.

“It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening. “The limitations of our two former spaces never stopped this museum from making important, historic, significant work, it never stopped people from coming and making this a place that was important to them, it never made it so that artists didn’t want to work or engage or show here.

It has been revealed that "However, what it meant to do those things in those spaces often required incredible effort and ingenuity because they weren’t spaces made to be museums, they weren’t spaces made for art. What this space does is it not only increases our physical space, but it allows us to work in ways that we could only dream of in those former spaces.”.

The Studio Museum reopened at 144 West 125th Street in 2025 Photo: © Dror Baldinger FAIA.

Golden’s history at the Studio Museum spans not only her 21 years as its director, but stretches back to her years as an undergraduate student of art history and African American studies at Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts, during which time she had an internship at the museum. After graduation, she stayed on as a curatorial fellow.

Industry observers note that her career then led her to the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she was initially a curatorial assistant, then the director of its off-site programme in Midtown Manhattan, and later an associate curator. During her time there she co-curated the influential 1993 Whitney Biennial (with Elisabeth Sussman) and curated Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art (1994-95), a landmark examination of the construction of Black masculinity through post-war art.

According to recent reports, golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000, when she was hired as the deputy director for exhibitions and programmes, collaborating with the then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. Golden took over the top job in 2005, when Sims stepped down. In addition to her curatorial projects—including a major Chris Ofili show in 2005 and a survey of figuration in African American Art (2002)—Golden became increasingly focused on building the Studio Museum’s future.

In a recent development, when preparations for demolition of its longtime home on 125th Street required the Studio Museum to close in 2018, Golden pursued partnerships with cultural and community organisations in Harlem. Building on a crucial professional development programme created with the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in 2015, she helped launch a multi-year partnership with MoMA and MoMA PS1 in 2019. This led to exhibitions of the Studio Museum’s collection and showcases for the participants in its renowned artist-in-residence programme at those institutions while construction was under way on the newly introduced building.

Construction of the Studio Museum’s new home was complicated by both the Covid-19 pandemic, which brought activity to a standstill, and by accusations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against its architect, David Adjaye. (He has denied all the allegations.) The site’s eventual completion and reopening, in November 2025, was seen as a triumph, creating a vastly expanded, purpose-built home for Black art that is equal to the museum’s ambitious programming and stellar permanent collection. The collection was significantly expanded during Golden’s tenure.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to fresh projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden noted in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of directors, trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences and beloved Harlem neighbours; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us.”.

As vital to Golden’s legacy at the Studio Museum as her leadership in the building project is how her work has elevated a latest generation of curators and institutional leaders, and championed artists of the African diaspora who had historically been overlooked. In her work at the Studio Museum and elsewhere, she has provided crucial support for artists including Amy Sherald, Lorna Simpson, Mark Bradford, Simone Leigh and Njideka Akunyili Crosby.

Recent findings suggest that “She has nurtured the careers of countless artists; she has impacted the arc of art history; she has overseen the construction of a world-class facility in Harlem; and she has transformed the way the public thinks about art of the African diaspora,” Darren Walker, the former president of the Ford Foundation, told The New York Times. (The Ford Foundation endowed the Studio Museum's director position through a $10m grant in 2024.).

According to recent reports, in addition to her role at the Studio Museum, Golden serves on the board of directors of the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation and the Obama Foundation.

A student photographer who lost his right eye after he was allegedly struck by a projectile fired by a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent while covering a “No Kings” protest is suing the federal government.

Warning: The following photos contain content that some may find upsetting.

Tucker Collins, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Southern California (USC), was left partially blind after photographing demonstrators in downtown Los Angeles on the afternoon of March 28. Collins was allegedly photographing a confrontation between protesters and federal agents when he was allegedly hit by a less-lethal projectile.

It has been revealed that footage shows Collins taking pictures of demonstrators outside a federal facility before suddenly falling to his knees as a crowd-control projectile reportedly struck him in the right eye, fracturing bones in his eye socket. Collins was taken to a hospital, where he underwent two and a half hours of surgery in an attempt to save the eye. The injury was too severe, and the eye was surgically removed.

Collins sued the federal government on Monday, alleging that law enforcement officers used excessive force and violated his civil rights. According to a report by The Upcoming York Times, his attorneys allege that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers “assaulted” and “used unjustified force against him” as he photographed the protest.

The lawsuit seeks various damages from the federal government, “including past and future medical expenses, prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, educational expenses, and loss of earning capacity.”.

It has been revealed that collins’s attorney, V. James DeSimone, and his family are also demanding criminal charges against the officer responsible for shooting him. They argue that the officer’s actions violated California law governing the use of projectile launchers by law enforcement.

The lawsuit also details how Collins’s injuries have limited his ability to pursue activities he once enjoyed, including photography. Collins indicates he is no longer able to safely photograph public events similar to the protest where he was injured. DeSimone also condemned the lack of criminal accountability in the wake of the shooting.

“It is deeply disturbing that the maiming of Tucker Collins, resulting in the loss of his eye, was widely reported and captured on video and, yet, there is no law enforcement response, to date, on the Federal, State or Local level to prosecute the offending officer for his crime,” DeSimone indicates in a statement. “Once again, it is left to civil rights attorneys to attempt to achieve some semblance of justice for the permanent and irreversible harm caused to this courageous young man.”.
